extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists, and researchers interested in Charlie Hebdo and satirical journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Principles, controversies, and legal/ethical considerations illustrated by Charlie Hebdo's practice of publishing provocative political and religious cartoons; useful for understanding limits and consequences of satire in a French/international context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy for freedom of expression and secularism
rubrics_metrics.description: Since its founding, Charlie Hebdo has been a vocal advocate for free expression and secularism, using satire to critique organized religion, political movements, and other centers of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames satire as a civic value and mission: justification for provocative material. Examples on the page: repeated caricatures of religion and politics, the 'Je Suis Charlie' movement after the 2015 attack, and editorial statements defending publication as part of a tradition of satire. Use as a criterion: does the piece engage with power/ideas (not just shock) and assert a free-expression rationale?

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal-opportunity satire / deliberate provocation
rubrics_metrics.description: "We do caricatures of everyone, and above all every week, and when we do it with the Prophet, it's called provocation." (editorial defence quoted on the page)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charlie Hebdo's editorial stance is to satirise all targets rather than single out one group; provocation is an explicit editorial aim. Guidance for producing/evaluating satire: check whether targets are treated with parity across religion/politics and whether provocation is intentional rather than gratuitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal boundary and contextual interpretation under French hate-speech law (Mosque of Paris v. Val)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The court followed the state attorney's reasoning that two of the three cartoons were not an attack on Islam, but on Muslim terrorists, and that the third cartoon ... should be seen in the context of the magazine in question, which attacked religious fundamentalism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or defending satirical material in France, consider whether the work targets extremist actors/ideologies versus a protected group as such, and whether context (magazine's history, accompanying text) supports a political/critical reading. The page gives the 2007 acquittal as an example and shows that legal outcomes hinge on target and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political/prudential advice to avoid gratuitously hurting convictions
rubrics_metrics.description: French President Jacques Chirac's statement cited on the page: "Anything that can hurt the convictions of someone else, in particular religious convictions, should be avoided."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses a public-policy/prudential standard (not a legal ruling). Use as an evaluative axis: assess likely public/political backlash and whether self-restraint would better serve public interest. The page juxtaposes this view with free-expression defences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mocking victims and tragedies (sensitivity to harm)
rubrics_metrics.description: The page documents backlash to covers that lampooned recent tragedies or victims (e.g., cartoons seen as mocking the dead in the Metrojet crash, the depiction of Alan Kurdi, earthquake-victims-as-pasta), provoking domestic and international outrage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: treating recent deaths or vulnerable victims as punchlines tends to generate substantial criticism and may undercut claims of principled satire. As a production/evaluation criterion, consider timing, target (victim vs perpetrator), and likely international reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between satire and racial/religious stereotyping (racism accusations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics and litigants accused some cartoons of making a link between Muslims and Muslim terrorists — "That has a name and it's called racism" — leading to lawsuits and public condemnation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether cartoons rely on or reinforce negative stereotypes of a protected group rather than criticising behaviours, ideologies, or extremists. The page cites legal suits and public responses illustrating that perceived racism can convert satire into alleged hate speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience, translation, and representational risk (misrepresentation abroad)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Daniel Schneidermann argues that the 2015 attack raised the profile of the paper internationally with non-Francophone audiences, meaning that only parts of the paper are selectively translated into English, making it easy to misrepresent the editorial stance of the publication and the purpose of provocative work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or judging satire intended for an international audience, consider selective translation and cultural context: fragments in translation can misrepresent intent. Criterion: assess how likely content is to be misinterpreted outside its original cultural/linguistic context and whether additional context should be provided.
